diagnostic_evidence.quote: Since the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:with_sigmaout_PreVersion} is a continuous function of $\wprod$ on $\R^\N$ by Assumptions \ref{as:A1}-\ref{as:A3}, it is locally Lipschitz continuous at any point.

This clearly contradicts the local uniqueness of the trajectory $\wprod$ since on $(\t_\star-\varepsilon,\t_\star)$ both the original trajectory $\gamma_1(\t) = \widetilde w_i(\t)$ and the constant trajectory $\gamma_2(\t) = \widetilde w_i(\t_\star)$ are solutions for \eqref{eq:with_sigmaout_PreVersion}.

issues.failure_explanation: Continuity of the vector field does not imply local Lipschitz continuity or uniqueness. Moreover, fixing one coordinate at its boundary value does not generally produce a solution of the coupled vector ODE. Under the stated once-differentiable assumptions finite-time boundary crossing is possible; for example, a signed $|w|^{3/2}$ reparametrization has a Hölder, non-Lipschitz derivative at zero and admits solutions crossing zero.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Impose a genuine uniqueness or nonattainability condition, such as sufficient local Lipschitz regularity of the induced vector field, and replace the coordinatewise argument with a valid invariance proof.
issues.overall_effect: The domain invariance claim is false under the advertised regularity, and the implicit-bias argument relying on the trajectory staying where the inverse reparametrization and $h$ are defined is unsupported.
issues.title: Continuous differentiability does not prevent crossing the reparametrization boundary
issues.why_classification: A comparable theorem may survive after a contained regularity strengthening, but this withdraws the paper's emphasized once-continuously-differentiable scope.

issues.failure_explanation: Assumption A3 gives differentiability and a uniquely characterized zero value but not convexity. The key Bregman decay inequality uses the first-order convexity inequality for $L(\cdot,y)$. Without it, gradient flow can converge to a positive-loss stationary point, so neither the $O(1/t)$ loss decay nor convergence to a zero-loss point follows.
